1. The animation compares two kinds of payout check by what they can buy. A "level check" pays the same dollar amount every year. A "rising check" goes up over time. Both are measured against US consumer prices (CPI-U) from Aug 2006 to Aug 2026.

2. The "first check" line is a flat baseline. The level-check line starts on it and slides steadily downward, and a dotted marker at year 5 shows it at about 9 in 10 of its starting value. The rising-check line, drawn with dots, stays near the baseline for most of the 20 years. It dips a little at the end. A "?" appears in the last frames.

3. Rising prices shrink what a fixed payment can buy. After 5 years the level check buys about 90% of what it first did. After 20 years it buys much less. The rising check holds roughly the same buying power, and the caption says it is "there after 20 years". The "?" and the notes "ILLUSTRATIVE", "US only" and "history, not a forecast" say the past may not repeat.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. It shows the pattern and warns that it is only history.

5. None.
